## Application: OpenFlights Data {#sec-application}

::: {.section-subtitle}
The Pareto front of the transport between the two largest airports in the world
:::

To generate benchmarks with real data, we used the list of airports from the OpenFlights
database[^openflights]. We selected as initial airport and goal airport, the largest and second
largest airport, namely Hartsfield Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and Beijing Capital
International Airport (PEK). As central cities, we kept eleven large airports through which a
passenger can travel from ATL to PEK: Dubai (DXB), Munich (MUC), Frankfurt (FRA), Amsterdam
(AMS), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), Chicago O'Hare (ORD), Las Vegas (LAS),
Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), Denver (DEN) and Houston (IAH).

[^openflights]: [`airports.dat`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jpatokal/openflights/master/data/airports.dat)
of [OpenFlights](https://openflights.org/data.php), made available under the
[Open Database License](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/). The thirteen rows used
here are kept in
[`site/paper/data/atl-pek.coords`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/site/paper/data/atl-pek.coords),
with this attribution.

For each pair of airports, we calculated the spherical distance between the two airports, on a
sphere of radius 6,371 km, in units of 100 km rounded to integers. This distance is used for the
makespan. The cost of landing in an airport has been defined as follows: for a given airport
$C_i$, 1) compute the spherical distances $d_{\text{ATL},i}$ and $d_{i,\text{PEK}}$ between the
airport and respectively, ATL and PEK; 2) assign the inverse of the average distance, i.e.
$c_i = \frac{2}{d_{\text{ATL},i} + d_{i,\text{PEK}}}$, with the distances in km, multiplied by
$10^7$ and rounded to an integer (@tbl-airports).

| Airport | $d_i$ (km) | $\bar d_i$ (km) | $c_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dubai (DXB) | 12,200 | 5,800 | 1,108 |
| Munich (MUC) | 7,700 | 7,700 | 1,297 |
| Frankfurt (FRA) | 7,400 | 7,800 | 1,316 |
| Amsterdam (AMS) | 7,100 | 7,800 | 1,343 |
| San Francisco (SFO) | 3,400 | 9,500 | 1,547 |
| Seattle (SEA) | 3,500 | 8,700 | 1,641 |
| Chicago O'Hare (ORD) | 1,000 | 10,600 | 1,733 |
| Las Vegas (LAS) | 2,800 | 10,000 | 1,558 |
| Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) | 1,200 | 11,200 | 1,617 |
| Denver (DEN) | 1,900 | 10,200 | 1,650 |
| Houston (IAH) | 1,100 | 11,600 | 1,579 |

: The central cities: spherical distance $d_i$ from ATL and $\bar d_i$ to PEK, as used by the solver, and landing cost $c_i$. {#tbl-airports}

Of course, in this example, the cost was set up arbitrarily and does not reflect any real cost
but one can imagine that the cost is defined to represent some tax, or a sort of risk, i.e.
linked with a certain infectious disease or an on-going conflict. As it decreases with the length
of the detour, the fastest airports are the most expensive ones: Chicago lies on the great circle
from ATL to PEK, so that ATL → ORD → PEK is as short as a direct flight, while Dubai is the
cheapest airport and the slowest.

The instance is non-symmetric, since the initial and the goal cities are apart. Flights between
two central airports raise the question of [the previous sections](#sec-short):
their spherical distances satisfy the triangular inequality (AΔ), but they are much shorter than
a detour through ATL or PEK (SFO and SEA are 1,100 km apart, while the shortest detour between
them, through ATL, is 6,900 km long), so (A1-NS) fails. We therefore study two versions of the
instance:

* *hub and spoke*: a plane flies only between ATL or PEK and a central airport. A flight between
  two central airports is then never faster than a detour through ATL or PEK, (A1-NS) holds, and
  by {{< node "Corollary 6.10" >}} the Pareto front is the Pareto set of (cost, least makespan)
  over role configurations;
* *direct flights*: every pair of airports is joined by a flight of their spherical distance.

### The hub and spoke instance {#sec-hub}

We solved the instance with $t = 6$ travelers and $p$ from 2 to 5 planes
(@fig-airports). For $p = 3$, 4 and 5, ZenoSolver closes every gap of its bracket and the
Pareto front is exact, under (A1-NS): it returns a certificate of format version 2, which
`zeno check` accepts, assuming (A1-NS). Each run takes less than half a second. For $p = 2$, the
solver certifies 115 of the 217 gaps between its 218 achieved points, in 30 s; on the other 102,
its exact program for balanced role configurations exceeds its built-in limits, and the front is
only bracketed: every achieved point is reached by a plan, and in each open gap the cheapest plan
costs at most the achieved cost and at least the lower bound the solver reports, which differ by
0.2% on average and by 1.1% at most.

As expected, the front is composed of fewer points when the number of planes increases, as
reported in @fig-airports.

The Pareto fronts of the hub and spoke instance with $t = 6$ travelers and $p$ from 2 to 5
planes, as (makespan, cost). The fronts for $p = 3$, 4 and 5 are exact. For $p = 2$ the points
are the achieved ones, and an orange point opens a gap that no lower bound closes. Each panel
spans its own ranges.
:::

The instance with 6 travelers and 3 planes has a Pareto front made of 103 distinct objective
vectors. The two extreme points (Cost, Makespan) are $(15597, 34800)$ and $(9972, 54000)$. These
two points are obtained by using exclusively one airport, either Chicago (ORD) or Dubai (DXB), and
do not perform any $(B\bar B)$-pairing:

```
C. 15597 Mk. 34800
ATL -> ORD -> PEK -> ORD -> ATL -> ORD -> PEK
ATL -> ORD -> PEK -> ORD -> ATL -> ORD -> PEK
ATL -> ORD -> PEK -> ORD -> ATL -> ORD -> PEK
```

```
C. 9972 Mk. 54000
ATL -> DXB -> PEK -> DXB -> ATL -> DXB -> PEK
ATL -> DXB -> PEK -> DXB -> ATL -> DXB -> PEK
ATL -> DXB -> PEK -> DXB -> ATL -> DXB -> PEK
```

However, there are non-dominated plans using other airports, notably Amsterdam (AMS) and Munich
(MUC), and performing $(B\bar B)$-pairings, 18 of the 103 points in all. In the following plan,
the second plane leaves a passenger in AMS and another in MUC, and the third plane one in AMS;
the first plane takes the two passengers left in AMS to PEK, and the third plane the one left in
MUC:

```
C. 11479 Mk. 47600
ATL -> MUC -> PEK -> AMS -> PEK -> AMS -> PEK
ATL -> AMS -> ATL -> MUC -> ATL -> DXB -> PEK
ATL -> AMS -> ATL -> DXB -> PEK -> MUC -> PEK
```

Finally, for some Pareto optimal plan, planes do not always perform the same number of flights:

```
C. 13162 Mk. 41700
ATL -> SFO -> ATL -> AMS -> PEK -> LAS -> PEK
ATL -> IAH -> ATL -> LAS -> ATL -> AMS -> PEK -> SFO -> PEK
ATL -> DXB -> PEK -> IAH -> PEK
```

The plans were printed by `zeno --plans`, which checks each of them by simulation; makespans are
in km.

### The instance with direct flights {#sec-direct}

With direct flights between the central airports, the plans above remain feasible, and ZenoSolver
finds the same achieved points. It certifies none of the gaps, however: (A1-NS) fails, and the
only lower bound it uses that holds for every table of central flights, the relaxation of
{{< node "Lemma 3.4" >}} with each landing in $C_i$ weighing $2\min(d_i, \bar d_i)$, is too weak
here. Another bound holds with no assumption at all: by {{< node "Lemma 6.19" >}}, every plan has
a makespan of at least $(2t - p)\Phi/p$, where $\Phi = 11{,}600$ km, in the rounded distances, is
the shortest flight time from ATL to PEK, through Chicago. For $p = 2$ and
$p = 3$ this is 58,000 km and 34,800 km, the makespans of the fastest achieved points, so these
makespans are exact even with direct flights. Whether direct flights lower the cost of other
points is open. They may: the airports close to ATL are far from PEK and conversely, so that $d$
and $\bar d$ order the cities in opposite ways, which is the situation in which a flight between
central cities can beat every plan of simple patterns ({{< node "Proposition 6.7" >}}).

### Reproducing the instance {#sec-reproduce}

The data files are in
[`site/paper/data/`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/tree/master/site/paper/data):
`atl-pek.coords` (the coordinates), `atl-pek-direct.dat` (durations, costs and the table of
direct flights) and `atl-pek.dat` (the hub and spoke instance, without that table, so that
ZenoSolver gives the flights between central cities a duration longer than any detour).

```sh
# durations from the coordinates, in units of 100 km (-r 0.01); the third line of the
# generated file (the costs) is then replaced by the costs of the table above
zeno generate --metric sphere --hubs apart --coords atl-pek.coords -n 11 -r 0.01 -O atl-pek-direct.dat
zeno -d atl-pek.dat -n 11 -t 6 -p 3 --plans --certificate atl-pek-p3.cert
zeno check atl-pek-p3.cert
zeno -d atl-pek-direct.dat -n 11 -t 6 -p 3
```
